data.title: My father-in-law, 81, sold his $75,000 home to pay his daughter's $50,000 debt. How can I keep him from becoming destitute?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'Nothing has been set aside for his needs'

"I can see a very real possibility that my husband and I will eventually be expected to step in and provide financial support." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My 81-year-old father-in-law sold the family home in July for $75,000. For context, this is in a small town in Illinois, and the house was purchased in 1972 for approximately $7,500. Will he owe capital-gains taxes on the sale when he files his taxes next year?

Taking this a step further, he paid off all of his own bills and then paid off $50,000 of my sister-in-law's debt. I'm also curious about the potential tax implications for her as well. What concerns me most is that the money is gone, and nothing has been set aside for his needs.

I can see a very real possibility that my husband and I will eventually be expected to step in and provide financial support. I'm trying to understand the potential tax consequences, but I'm concerned about the bigger picture.

What happens when the money runs out and he needs financial assistance?

The Daughter-in-Law

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?

Housing instability is one of the most costly and unpredictable problems an elderly person can face.

Dear Daughter-in-Law,

Nothing about your letter inspires confidence in your father-in-law's confusing and, frankly, murky situation.

I'm afraid your father-in-law traded away his financial security. Housing instability is one of the most costly and unpredictable problems an elderly person can face. I have so many questions and concerns. Among them: Did he sell the family home to pay off his daughter's debt? Is he living with his formerly indebted daughter? Or does he have another home where he is living? Is he living solely off his Social Security? When did you discover that he had paid off his daughter's $50,000 debt? Has she agreed to a plan to repay him?

Making sure your father-in-law has a safe and secure place to live is the No. 1 priority. I assume he is relying on Social Security, for his immediate financial needs and Medicare for his medical needs. Medicaid could be an option, going forward. Selling his only home does not automatically violate the Medicaid five-year lookback rule, provided he sold it for fair market value, and neither does paying his own debts. However, he paid off his daughter's $50,000 debt, which actually could trigger the lookback rule.

"The state will look at financial transactions made during the 60 months (or five years) before they applied for Medicaid for long-term care," according to Illinois Legal Aid. "During this period, the state checks whether the applicant or their spouse gave away money or property, sold something for less than its fair market value, made property transfers into trusts, or created new annuities. If these types of transfers happened during the look-back period, a person can't get Medicaid for a certain amount of time. This is known as a 'penalty period.' "

Related: 'Some people did everything right': I lost my home in the Great Recession. I rent in my 50s. Why is that judged as failure?

Alarm bells

Taxes are probably the least of your concerns. Your father-in-law's capital gain on the home sale is well below the applicable exclusion. If this were a larger house sale in a major metropolitan area, you can exclude $250,000 in capital gains as a single person (or $500,000 for a married couple) from your taxable income. He won't owe tax on the $50,000 gift, but he will have to file a federal gift-tax return Form 709 as there is a $19,000 annual limit ($38,000 for a married couple) for such gifts before you must report it. Still, it's well below the lifetime exemption.

Any sequence of events that leads a person, especially someone like your father-in-law who is 81 years old, to effectively make himself penniless and dependent on others raises serious alarm bells. Did your sister-in-law coerce or somehow pressure him into paying off her $50,000 debt? Have you had a family meeting about these financial transactions? I can only hope that he has moved in with her or has a second home where he can live. If you are concerned about his welfare, it's time for a family meeting.

There's a significant difference, legally and morally, between financial mismanagement and elder financial abuse. During your meeting, I implore you to find out whether he understood that he was giving away $50,000 instead of giving his daughter a loan, and whether the decision to do so was a voluntary one. Does he currently have control of his bank account, or are there any co-signers or, more alarmingly, co-owners on those accounts? I would not rule out reaching out for third-party help, if you suspect your father-in-law was an unwitting participant.

Third-party help includes Section 8 housing, which has eligibility requirements and waiting lists; senior housing; and subsidized apartments. Organizations worth contacting include the Illinois Department of Aging, which should be able to direct you toward legal counsel; the National Center on Elder Abuse, an agency affiliated with the U.S. Administration on Aging; the National Council on Aging advocacy group; AARP's Fraud Watch Network Helpline at (877) 908-3360; the National Elder Fraud Hotline at (833) 372-8311; and Adult Protective Services.

Illinois does not have filial responsibility laws, so adult children are not financially responsible for their parents. Given that you are concerned, however, your work may have only just begun.

Related: Building U.S. data centers is getting so expensive that AI companies are moving overseas

data.title: 'She's living the dream': My stepmother said I can buy my childhood home for $850,000. Is she taking advantage of me?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s'

"She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s. By the time he died, it was worth about $850,000, mostly because it's spacious and in a good neighborhood. He left it to my stepmother, whom he married a few years after my mom died. She is now 74. They were together for 18 years. She took care of him through the whole illness, which I don't take lightly.

Dad told me more than once that the house would be mine someday. My stepmother now wants to sell and move somewhere smaller. She's living the dream in Miami. I offered $700,000. That's $200,000 under market, but I thought it was fair, given that she would skip agent fees and it would be a quick, clean sale. I'd have to stretch to do it, but I could manage.

She was really offended, and she told me as much. She said she's paid the property taxes and the repairs for years (she put a new roof on in 2021). She also said she spent a big chunk of her own savings on my father's care and that the house is basically her retirement plan, and that she can't just hand me $200,000 because I'm sentimental.

Don't miss: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?

The $200,000 discount

That's a fair point, and I told her so. What I can't get past is that a few years ago she gave her daughter $200,000 toward a house, and that is how (and why) I came up with the $200,000 haircut on my father's home. I brought that up, and she said things were different then, and pointed out that I have a good job and can buy my own place.

She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died. As my girlfriend at the time said, "Yes, she really went there." That comment really stung. He trusted her with everything, and it feels like his wishes just evaporated. She says she honored him by caring for him and that I'm discounting everything she sacrificed.

I could, of course, walk away and buy somewhere else. I've even looked at a couple of listings. But it wouldn't be the same, and I'd always feel like the house slipped away from our family. I know that my stepsister's place has a sauna in the basement, and I'd bet anything that my stepmother helped pay for that too. Not that I'm keeping score. (OK, I know I am a little.)

Am I being unreasonable?

The Stepson

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?

You can't force someone to sell you a house that never legally belonged to you.

Dear Stepson,

Don't allow steam from your stepsister's sauna to cloud your vision. You can grieve the loss of your childhood home without assigning blame.

What's more, you can't force someone to sell you a house that never belonged to you in the first place. Your childhood home, legally and morally, belonged to your father. Even though you grew up there, that doesn't give you the right to a life estate or a $200,000 discount on the purchase price because your stepmother gave her daughter $200,000 toward the down payment on her own home. What's more, selling a house to a family member below fair market value can create a gift of equity equal to the price difference, which the IRS may treat as a taxable gift.

Your late father made a promise that he did not keep, could not keep or decided not to keep. That was his responsibility. It's not your stepmother's job to make good on your father's promises. Whether he made a will leaving her the house or whether she inherited the house through state intestate laws, the end result is the same: She legally owns the house, and she has the right to live there or sell it to whomever she wants.

It is your belief that your father's wishes "evaporated." But wishes, promises and/or intentions evolve, and perhaps he realized that he wanted to take care of his wife of nearly two decades, and die with the knowledge that she would always have a roof over her head. It would have been better to have discussed those plans with you rather than leaving you in a kind of limbo, wondering if he truly wanted to leave his estate to his wife. Chances are, he did.

That does not mean this is an easy or pleasant situation for you. You have an emotional attachment to this property, and you regard your stepmother as an interloper, inheriting a property where your own mother probably once lived. It's a tough break for you and your siblings, if you have any. You made your stepmother an offer and she declined. She may be thinking about her own retirement and financial future.

Don't miss: 'I don't feel sorry for myself': I'm 64 and will be renting for the rest of my life. Is that so bad?

Passing judgment

Two decades is a long time to spend with someone. She met your father when she was in her 50s, and she's now rightly concerned about medical costs, if she needs nursing home care, especially if she does not have long-term care insurance, or any other kind of life insurance. This house may be the only asset she has, and downsizing will give her a cushion as she heads towards her 80th birthday in six years. That's quite a reality check.

I'm heartened that you realize that taking care of your father was no small deal for your stepmother. Who will take care of her if she sells you this house for $650,000 and runs out of money? Will you drive her to hospital appointments and spend hours a day with her, making sure that she takes her medication and pays her bills, and has enough to eat? That might sound dramatic, but getting older often comes with health complications.

One could argue that you both "went there." She "went there" by telling you your father wanted her to have his house. You "went there" by using emotional leverage, whether or not you believe it in your heart to be valid, to persuade her to sell this house to you on the cheap. By doing so, you are, whether you realize it or not, also passing judgment on her marriage of 18 years to a man she probably loved very much. You both spoke plainly. That's OK. Just know it's 50/50.

If you want this house, put in an offer when it is listed for sale. If she does get more than one offer and, say, one party offers $50,000 more, she may still decide to sell you the house (and maybe not even mention that she is selling it to you at less than the other offer). Remember, if she gets $950,000 rather than $850,000 - a real possibility if it's a cash buyer and it's a sought-after neighborhood - she would have been giving you a $300,000 discount if she agreed to your proposal.

All is fair in love, second marriages, legal beneficiaries and real estate. Just don't overstretch yourself financially for the sake of nostalgia.

Related: 'People in the U.S. need to wake up': As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected applications from wealthy couples. Here's why.

data.title: My husband wants to sell our $1.5 million home and invest the proceeds. But this is where we raised our kids - and I can't bear to leave.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'He wants to buy something for $600,000 now that we are empty-nesters'

"We have another $1.8 million in retirement accounts and savings, plus Social Security." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm 67, my husband is 69, and we've been married 38 years. We've lived in the same four-bedroom colonial for 32 of those years. It's paid off and worth $1.5 million. We have another $1.8 million in retirement accounts and savings, plus Social Security and a small pension from his old job. No debt, and our kids are on their own.

So this isn't a money problem, but we can't talk about retirement anymore without it turning into a fight. He wants to buy something for $600,000 now that we are empty-nesters, and invest the rest. He has a spreadsheet. I've seen it open on the laptop at the kitchen table at 11 p.m., with property taxes, insurance and the lawn guy all in little columns.

He says we're heating rooms nobody uses, and he's right that nobody has slept in the fourth bedroom since our youngest left 12 years ago. It holds a treadmill (of course) and about nine boxes of Christmas decorations. He's also right that the place is a money pit. The roof has maybe three years left and the furnace sounds like it's clearing its throat every morning.

Last spring, we dropped $18,000 on a sewer line. Every time something breaks, Ron looks at me across the room like the case is closed. But the pantry door has pencil marks on it, one for every kid every year, with the dates in my handwriting. We brought both babies home to this house. He calls it sentimental clutter. I thought that was mean.

He slipped on the back steps last winter, and we both pretended it didn't scare us, but he could have just as easily slipped on another stairwell. All three kids live within an hour away. We host Thanksgiving every year, 14 people if everyone shows up, and the grandkids spend half of it out in the yard. Our daughter said she'd be sad if we sold.

I worry a small kitchen means the end of Thanksgiving, and that the grandkids will come less often if there's no yard. Ron says I'm inventing reasons because I'm scared of change. Maybe I am. But I don't want to be 75 and regret that we gave it up too soon. How do we decide whether staying is worth what it costs? Is it foolish to keep a house this big?

A Sentimental 67-Year-Old Homeowner

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I am a pretty cautious person': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?

I agree with your husband. I agree with you. Honestly, it's a tough call.

Dear Sentimental,

Take the pantry door with you when you go.

Joking aside, I think that's an idea worth exploring. Take whatever has sentimental value to your new home. If you live in a large, drafty house that costs money to heat, costs you thousands of dollars a year in property taxes and insurance, and you're only using a small number of rooms, it may no longer make financial sense to stay. But plenty of people live in the house where they raised their family because they love the house, the garden, and the feeling they get when they close the front door behind them. That's worth a lot.

It's as much a "money problem" as it is an everything-else problem. You have Social Security, which I'll assume is $4,000 a month between the two of you. If you follow the 4% rule and withdraw from your $1.8 million in savings in the first year, that would give you $72,000 before taxes. Whether your savings could endure that level of withdrawals over the rest of your lives depends on how much you spend, how you invest your nest egg, what happens in the stock market, how much you get in Social Security, and your husband's pension.

Your retirement fund could last until you're in your 90s, or for another 30 years (to be gloriously optimistic). An $80,000 income from $1.8 million equates to a 4.44% withdrawal rate in the first year, while an initial 4% withdrawal, adjusted for inflation in subsequent years, would give you $72,000 in the first year. You know your own lifestyle best, but this should give you a pretty good idea if you will need to downsize later. If you sold your house for $1.5 million and bought another for half the price, that would be a nice profit. You can afford to stay. You have choices.

There's plenty of room for discussion between his computer spreadsheet and your very real love for this place you call home. For starters, a lot of thought and time probably went into that spreadsheet. It may be his way of trying to make the next stage of your lives more secure. If you ended up with $2.7 million in investable assets after selling your home and buying another, a 4% initial withdrawal would - or could - give you an income of $108,000 a year before taxes. Would that difference affect how you want to live in retirement?

Related: My wife says we can't afford to retire, yet she wants to take an $8,000 trip to Italy. We have $4 million. Do I keep working?

A trial move

Moving makes more sense if you believe it would be expensive or impractical to future-proof your current home, with bedrooms and a decent bathroom on the ground floor. The costs of maintaining the house and your ability to live there safely as you age all matter. I agree with both of you that $18,000 for a sewer line is a lot of money, and that money could have been spent on a golf-club membership or several trips to Europe or South America. I agree with your husband. I agree with you. Honestly, it's a tough call.

What's the point of moving if one of you is unhappy? It's hard to imagine handing your home over to another couple or family and settling into a smaller space. If you talk to anyone who has lived in several properties throughout their life, they will probably have one home they still think about fondly. But it's "our" belongings - clothing, artwork, knickknacks, and all the stuff we accumulate (and get rid of as the years progress) - that create and, yes, recreate that familiar space that feels like home.

Explore your options with the help of a financial adviser, a couples therapist, or both. The former can help you compare the costs of staying versus going, while the latter can help you see each other's viewpoints. Once you have more clarity, an open discussion with your children could also help - not to get their approval, but to get their perspective. They know your family dynamics well and may have ideas. The starting point is that there is no "he's right and I'm wrong" or "I'm wrong and he's actually right." You both have valid points.

Rather than renting out your home or having strangers live among your belongings, why not spend some time in a rental property that could substitute as a long-term home. Visit open houses and imagine your life outside of this house, including during Thanksgiving and visits from your grandkids. It wouldn't hurt to have a survey done on your home to see how much you might have to pay for upgrades. You and your husband are not on opposing sides. You're on the same side. Just because he wants to downsize does not mean that he doesn't love the memories, too.

Related: My sister moved in with our mother, 78, and now says she deserves the $925,000 family home. Is she right?

data.title: Young Americans are giving up on car -2-
data.description:
"Younger and less affluent buyers have largely left the new-vehicle market," Sam Fiorani, vice president of global vehicle forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, told MarketWatch. At the moment, the U.S. car industry lacks options below $30,000. The loss of entry-level models such as the Ford Focus, Chevrolet Cruze and Nissan Versa over the past decade has "eliminated several key products that brought first-time buyers into the market," he noted.

Historically, "whenever the U.S. market moved too far upmarket, a new competitor helped rebalance prices," Fiorani said. "In the 1950s, it was Volkswagen. In the 1960s, it was Toyota, followed by Honda in the 1970s. Hyundai arrived in the 1980s, followed by Kia in the 1990s."

However, protectionist regulations and tariffs are currently preventing lower-cost cars from China from entering the U.S. market, eliminating a potential source of entry-level vehicles, he said.

From the archives (April 2026): Americans would love this $25,000 hybrid SUV - but it's not available here yet

It's hard for car companies to "make money on vehicles" that cost less than $30,000 now, Tom Libby, director of loyalty solutions and industry analysis at Mobility Global, told MarketWatch, but recent developments show there is consumer demand.

The Ford Maverick, unveiled in 2021 at $20,000, has "done very, very, very well," he said. It now costs $30,000.

Meanwhile, Slate Auto, the new electric-vehicle startup backed by Jeff Bezos, is taking preorders for trucks with roll-up windows that start at $25,000.

Even at lower prices, car makers will have to confront young consumers who are looking for alternatives to ownership. Dominic Berardi, a 21-year-old student in Orlando, Fla., has a car, but moved downtown and got a job as a server close by "because I was already planning to restructure my life around the transit that exists here, if at all possible."

For Berardi, independence no longer means having a car waiting outside. It means freedom from reliance on one.

data.title: Young Americans are giving up on car ownership. It's a path to financial freedom for some.
data.description:
By Venessa Wong

With vehicle prices soaring and ownership increasingly out of reach, some young adults are discovering that life without a car leaves them with breathing room to spend on other things

The average car has gotten so expensive that giving one up can provide young Americans with greater control over how they spend their money.

When Nick Renteria moved from Boston to Los Angeles for school, he rented a car for about $350 a month. His parents covered the rental cost while he paid for gas, but he hated sitting in traffic, parking and feeling disconnected from the city.

When he finished his program, Renteria, 24, decided he didn't want a car at all.

He moved to West Hollywood, selecting a neighborhood where he could bike to work, use public transportation and altogether avoid the expense of owning a vehicle.

The decision has paid off over the past two years. While a roommate with a car and a similar income struggled financially, Renteria found he could afford to go out with friends and enjoy the city, even while working part-time jobs.

"L.A. is actually kind of affordable if you don't have a car," he said.

For generations of Americans, owning a car has often been a symbol of independence. But, for some younger adults today, that notion is being turned on its head. The average car has gotten so expensive that giving one up can sometimes translate into gaining something equally important: greater control of how they spend their money.

"L.A. is actually kind of affordable if you don't have a car," said Nick Renteria, who went car-free two years ago.

And there are signs that younger Americans are shifting away from car ownership as a symbol of success.

The share of households younger than 35 that owned a vehicle last year fell to 79.4% from 82.1% in 2019, according to data from the Federal Reserve. Meanwhile, over the same period, vehicle ownership among Americans 75 and older rose to 83% from 80.1%. Younger adults have replaced the oldest Americans as the demographic with the lowest vehicle-ownership rate.

Other data suggest that young people are changing how they get around. Among adults 29 and younger, 48% drove themselves in their own car at least once a month this year, down from 53% in 2023, according to YouGov surveys. Meanwhile the share who rode as passengers increased to 54% from 45%. This was the only method of transportation to become more common among Generation Z adults during this period.

Those surveys gauge transportation habits and not necessarily car ownership. But, taken together with the ownership data, they point to a shift in the relationship between young Americans and personal motor vehicles.

The high cost of car ownership

The financial case for young Americans not owning a car is becoming increasingly compelling.

As the rising cost of vehicles, maintenance, insurance and loan payments deter young Americans from buying cars, many are migrating toward ride-sharing, carpooling and car-sharing options, and using delivery services, instead - and some say they prefer those alternatives to having a car of their own.

New vehicles now sell for more than $50,000, on average, and used cars for $27,000. Meanwhile, those who finance their vehicles face average interest rates of 6.35% for new cars and 11.19% for used cars, pushing up the average monthly payment to $765 for new cars and $542 for used cars, according to Experian.

And purchasing a car is only the beginning. Maintenance and insurance costs have increased dramatically since the pandemic, while gas prices have crossed $4 a gallon, on average, this year due to the war in Iran.

The average annual cost to own and operate a new vehicle is now $12,863, according to AAA.

More on this: Cars have become unaffordable for many Americans. Here's what the numbers show.

For younger Americans navigating a difficult job market, expensive housing and student-loan debt can consume a substantial chunk of income.

In a 2025 survey, common concerns hindering Gen Zers from buying a car included not being able to afford the type of car they wanted (30%), interest rates being too high (32%) and costly maintenance (28%), data shared with MarketWatch by Enterprise Mobility show.

On top of that, remote work and online shopping trends, as well as the proliferation of new delivery services, make it easier to forgo car ownership.

Last month, about one out of five workers ages 25 to 34 worked from home at least some of the time, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Meanwhile, Gen Z adults said online shopping (54%) and working from home (48%) have reduced their need to drive over the past few years, and more than 20% cited rideshare services, according to a Mercury Insurance survey in June.

In a separate poll, 29% of Gen Z members said they have used peer-to-peer car-sharing platforms, and, among them, 43% did so at least biweekly or monthly. Convenience and cost savings were the top reasons given among all survey respondents.

To these young Americans, such options have made owning a car a luxury, not a necessity.

For Xenna Smith, 27, selling her Subaru in Raleigh, N.C., last year was partly a money decision and partly about peace of mind. "I just felt a lot of anxiety," she told MarketWatch.

In addition to safety concerns as driver, "it was just costs and costs and costs," she said.

Now, Smith bikes or rides the bus almost anywhere she needs to go, and walks to buy groceries. Her apartment, which costs $1,500 a month, has a gym, a pool and bike parking.

In a typical month, she now spends less than $40 on transportation for the occasional Lyft and bike maintenance, compared with $600 when she had a car. Through a $25 annual membership at bike advocacy group Oaks and Spokes, she gets her bus pass for free.

While renting a car, ride-hailing apps (like Uber and Lyft), and public transit all come with their own costs, average transportation spending for households with no cars are lower at every income level - including the top 20% of earners - compared with households that own or lease at least one automobile, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

'I can afford my student loans now, my rent's comfortable, and I actually am saving money for once.'Xenna Smith, Raleigh, N.C.

There are tradeoffs. Not having a car makes it harder to see people who live out of town and can require extra effort and be physically demanding, Smith said. She also said she wished drivers would "stop being so aggressive to cyclists."

On the other hand, "I can afford my student loans now, my rent's comfortable and I actually am saving money for once," she said of having gone car-free. "I'm not contributing anything bad to the environment, and I'm making myself better physically."

Smith's experience underscores an important point: Going without a car isn't necessarily about giving something up. For some, it's about deciding what they would rather be able to afford.

When Sabrina Rae Santoro, a 33-year-old entrepreneur, moved from northern Scottsdale, Ariz., to Old Town Scottsdale earlier this year, she decided to give up her Mercedes. The loan payment, insurance, gas and maintenance cost about $1,000 each month, but she was only using the car to drive 20 to 30 miles each week because she normally works from home.

"Anybody that knows me knows, like, I am a car girly," Santoro said, but "I simply ran the numbers and worked out a location where everything that I need is pretty much five to 10 minutes away walking, or a short drive," she told MarketWatch.

Now, Santoro uses the on-site gym at home, has her groceries delivered, and shops on Amazon. To get around, she uses Lyft, which runs $450 to $500 a month. Compared with when she owned her car, "I'm spending half [as much on transportation], and the funny thing is, I still go everywhere I want to go. I don't limit myself," she said. "It's actually an improvement in quality of life. I feel free."

Sabrina Rae Santoro, a 33-year-old entrepreneur, decided to give up her Mercedes and says not owning a car has improved her quality of life. "I feel free," she told MarketWatch.

Living in cities with robust public transportation can ease the transition. "It's been a huge relief" financially and mentally to go car-free and not have to worry about maintenance and repairs, said D.J. Hargrave, a 30-year-old who sold his Honda when he moved to Chicago last year.

Hargrave's car expenses ran about $1,000 per month, and, when he sold his Accord Sport back to the dealership, he had to pay about $3,000 in negative equity.

Now, Hargrave relies on Chicago's network of buses and trains with a $75 monthly pass and spends less than $200 a month on Uber rides.

"Younger generations of consumers are doing a lot of math, and they don't believe that owning things is the way to go, or that they can ever own things to the same extent older generations have, so they make different choices," Jeremy Robb, chief economist at Cox Automotive, told MarketWatch.

As young people also delay getting married and have fewer children, "there are lifestyle choices that may mean they don't need to have a car, especially on the family side," Robb added.

Related: America's renter generation is trying to build wealth by investing in stocks instead of owning a house

Car-industry response

These transportation trends are showing up especially in sales of new cars. Drivers ages 18 to 34 made up 9.7% of new vehicle registrations in August, down from 12.7% five years earlier, according to automotive-data company Mobility Global.

data.title: I'm 58 and hate annuities. How can I get dependable income in retirement?
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

For a person looking to make their portfolio more conservative, a TIPS ladder may achieve the same effect

A TIPS ladder could complete part of your retirement income puzzle, but not all of it.

Got a question about retirement? Fill out our questionnaire or write to me directly at beth.pinsker@marketwatch.com (please put "Fix My Portfolio" in the subject line).

Dear Fix My Portfolio,

I will not buy annuities ...but I want a pretty dependable paycheck in retirement. How well would a TIPS ladder work?

I'm 58 and plan to work for seven more years (unless laid off earlier, which is also a constant concern these days). I want to try to hold off on Social Security until 70, so there will be a gap from 65 to 70 where I will need to depend on my portfolio more heavily.

I have mostly equities and it's probably time to fix that. So my plan would be to ladder a series of TIPS to provide income for the five-year gap. According to my calculations, I can put about a quarter of my money into defined maturity ETFs, where the ETF liquidates and shuts down in the year you buy it, so it's held until maturity. Or should I buy all five years now to lock in the current high real yield?

Once I get to 70, rental income and Social Security will likely not fund all of my income needs, so I'll need to spend more of my portfolio. For that, I was thinking I'd allocate another quarter to cash and ultrashort Treasury ETFs. Then the remaining half of the portfolio would be left to grow in equities.

Am I locking up too much money now instead of letting it grow another three or four years? My thinking is that it might not make my portfolio grow as much as it could if it were all equities, but it would give me a forever paycheck. If needed, I could still sell shares or I could stop reinvesting dividends.

I don't need to be wealthy. I just want to make sure I have what I need in retirement. And if I can leave something to my kids that would be great also.

Feeling TIPsy

Dear Feeling TIPsy,

People have very strong feelings about annuities - mostly negative. But as I recently discussed with Prudential's head of research, David Blanchett, insurance contracts for monthly checks solve a need that people say they want: guaranteed income in retirement. It's never too soon to start thinking about this, and 58 is definitely not on the early side for starting to implement a plan.

The reason you're a little queasy about being 90%-plus in equities all of a sudden is because your risk tolerance naturally tends to shift as you age. There's no right or wrong to that, because it's about your perceptions and what level of security helps you sleep at night. It makes sense mathematically, too, because you're going to stop work soon, and you have less time to make up for losses in the market.

If you're looking for guaranteed income in retirement, there are many ways to go. Annuities are one route, for sure, but that's a nonstarter with you. Another option is to shift your portfolio allocations toward more fixed income - Treasury products, corporate bonds, dividend stocks, cash instruments like CDs or even just high-yield savings accounts. You can mix and match as you see fit.

Leaning toward TIPS means one of your chief worries is inflation. TIPS are Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, and you can buy them directly from the government at issue at treasurydirect.gov, on the secondary market through brokers or in the form of ETFs or other funds. With these, you never lose your invested amount if you hold to maturity, but the principal value will fluctuate, along with the twice-yearly interest payment, according to the inflation rate at the time.

If you're looking for an easier option to understand than annuities, TIPS may not be the answer. "TIPS are complicated," said Jeremy Fletcher, a partner and head of trading at Asset Dedication, a firm that handles TIPS investments. As a chartered financial analyst and somebody who helped start one of the earliest TIPS mutual funds in the 1990s, Fletcher would know.

For laddering, Fletcher said that his team favors the kind of term-maturity ETFs you're talking about. "They mature each year around mid-October, so you get a similar experience to owning individual bonds," he said. Among the benefits, he liked that they could be bought in smaller quantities than buying direct, which can be helpful to individual investors, and that the management fees are minimal, usually around 10 basis points.

He did offer a few caveats, however: "The inflation accrual is passed through along with coupon interest on a quarterly basis; so if the payments are not reinvested, you don't get the full benefit of inflation protection," he said. Also, the ETFs only go out 10 years, while TIPS from the government can go out 30 years.

Also be mindful of where you hold your TIPS ladder, because there may be tax issues you're not aware of because of how and when the income hits your return each year.

If you're looking for more information, Fletcher suggested going to an online program like TIPSladder.com for help structuring, or to your brokerage of choice. All should have a calculator to help you construct a ladder with the timeline and budget that you would like.

Overall strategy

Your plan is to go from all-in on stocks to something more akin to 50-50, with your fixed-income side split between a TIPS ladder and short-term Treasurys. Doing that in one fell swoop might feel jarring to you. A more typical progression is to ratchet down to about 70% equities and 30% in fixed-income products, and then go from there. You could ladder TIPS, but also you could ladder CDs or just keep some funds in cash for emergencies, like being laid off.

You could also consider taking Social Security at 67 instead of 70, to avoid dipping too far into your principal in the years after you stop working. This is not a suggestion for action, but rather something worth running as a scenario. There are plenty of calculators available for figuring out your optimal claiming strategy. What you want to look for most is the difference between the lifetime increase in your Social Security payout at 67 compared with 70, and how that compares to taking that amount out of your portfolio. It could be that the ding to your savings is not worth it, but you'd need to see the actual numbers to know that for sure.

One last thing to think about is that you'll need to reset your TIPS ladders eventually, because they do not run for your entire lifespan. While the product is designed to protect you against inflation during the term you buy for, you will face reinvestment risk. You're young, and that could mean several cycles of ladders, and you don't know what inflation will be in 20 years.

You can also join the Retirement conversation in our Facebook community: Retire Better with MarketWatch.

-- Are we spending our retirement money in the right order? Our plan is: Social Security, annuities, cash-then IRA.

-- Worse than taking away your parents' car keys? Taking away their cellphone. How to protect your aging parents.

-Beth Pinsker

data.title: I want to pay off $4,500 in credit-card debt in 2 months. Is this possible?
data.description:
By Aditi Shrikant

'I'm 32 years old and feel like I should know how to do this stuff by now'

"Every time I get close to paying it off, I need to use my card for some medical bill or emergency expenses."

Dear Dollar Signs,

I cannot seem to get out of credit-card debt no matter what I do. It's not a lot - about $4,500 - but it's weighing on me. Every time I get close to paying it off, I need to use my card for some medical bill or emergency expenses. It feels like I'm never out of the hole. I'm 32 years old and feel like I should know how to do this stuff by now.

I have about $1,000 in savings, but I don't want to put that toward these emergencies because then I feel like I'll have nothing.

I'd love to pay this off by the end of the year. Do you have any tips?

Fiscally Flustered

If you're just starting out on your money or career journey and have questions about how to navigate your finances, we want to hear from you. Write to Dollar Signs, MarketWatch's new advice column, at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

Dear Flustered,

I feel for you. A relatively low amount of credit-card debt can be easy to neglect - and I've definitely done it myself. But putting it off and carrying a balance will, as I'm sure you know, negatively affect your credit score. And the interest on your balance ensures that even if you stop making purchases, your debt will grow. It doesn't help that credit-card APRs have been going up in recent years, making credit-card debt more expensive.

I'll be honest: I don't think you'll be able to pay this off by the end of the year. There are 10 weeks left in 2026, meaning you'd have to direct $450 a week (not including interest) to this debt. That is a lot of money, and I assume if you were earning enough to do this, you would have by now. This will take a bit longer.

You need a six- to 12-month "financial reset," according to Mark La Spisa, a certified financial planner based in Barrington, Ill.

You are right not to touch that $1,000. Keep it as an emergency reserve and work on allocating some of your monthly cash flow toward your debt. After you pay for your housing, groceries and utilities, how much money is left and what is it going toward? Most people are not spending all their disposable income wisely. The best way to find out where exactly you can cut spending is to look at your bank statements for the last 90 days.

"I'd specifically look for $300- to $500-per-month expenses that can temporarily be redirected toward the cards," La Spisa said.

Perhaps you order a lot of takeout food or call ride-hailing services frequently. Redirect those funds to your credit-card bill. I often find that I'm subscribed to far more streaming services than I actually use.

Once you decide the amount of money you want to put toward this bill each month, automate payments on payday. Don't even let the money hit your checking account.

Any random windfalls, such as a tax refund or work bonus, should also go toward paying off your credit-card bill.

"Look for one-time accelerators," La Spisa said. "A $4,000 problem can often be solved surprisingly quickly."

I know this can be hard. I often justify impulse purchases by telling myself that my money is supposed to bring me some happiness. While this is true, I can never truly enjoy a nice meal out or a new pair of shoes if any amount of debt is hanging over my head.

"We're not asking you to live this way forever," La Spisa said. "We're going to live differently for several months so you can stop carrying this debt forever."

How to become more financially aware

I do find it concerning that you don't know where to start when it comes to paying down this debt. To me, this signals that you aren't very aware of where your money is going.

Your first priority should be to pay off this $4,500, but the work doesn't stop there. You want to build and practice healthy spending habits, so that you don't end up in this position again and you can continue to build up your emergency savings fund. Experts recommend you have six months to a year worth of expenses saved.

"The real victory isn't paying off the $4,000," La Spisa said. "It's turning the $400 to $600 a month they were sending to credit-card companies into a permanent savings habit. That can materially change their long-term financial trajectory."

Research suggests that having $2,000 in cash saved for emergencies can meaningfully improve your sense of financial stability.

The exercise of reviewing your bank statements isn't a one-time thing. Regularly re-evaluate where your money is going, and what you need and enjoy.

You are young, and this isn't a crushing amount of debt. If you create a realistic budget and learn to live within it, you'll be able to pay off your debt and become a more savvy spender and saver.

Write to Dollar Signs at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

DIRECTV Adds NHL's New Carolina Hurricanes, Columbus Blue Jackets, Minnesota Wild, and St. Louis Blues Regional Channels

DIRECTV Adds NHL's New Carolina Hurricanes, Columbus Blue Jackets, Minnesota Wild, and St. Louis Blues Regional Channels

PR Newswire

EL SEGUNDO, Calif., Oct. 24, 2026

EL SEGUNDO, Calif., Oct. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DIRECTV today announced a new multi-year distribution agreement with the National Hockey League for Hurricanes Hockey Network, Blue Jackets Hockey Network, Wild+, and Blue Note+ pregame, postgame, and in-game live sports services.

Each of the four channels will be available to DIRECTV streaming and satellite customers who live in each team's NHL-designated home territory and subscribe to Choice and higher packages, and each U-verse customer in those same regions who subscribes to U200 and above.

This agreement also provides distribution rights to each NHL team to all of DIRECTV FOR BUSINESS's thousands of sports bars, restaurants, fitness clubs, and other commercial venues located within each team's respective region.

DIRECTV has recently obtained regional or local rights to provide 76 of the 81 U.S.-based NHL, NBA, or MLB franchises to their local fans, including multi-year agreements for 23 U.S.-based hockey teams.

"We are committed to keeping fans connected to their favorite teams and giving them more choice and flexibility in how they watch and what they pay," said Rob Thun, Chief Content Officer at DIRECTV. "As local sports distribution evolves, DIRECTV brings team channels, regional sports networks, and other viewing options together to make it easier for fans to follow the teams they love. We're pleased to work with the NHL, NBA, MLB, and others to deliver that experience."

"We're thrilled that fans of the Carolina Hurricanes, Columbus Blue Jackets, Minnesota Wild, and St. Louis Blues can now watch their favorite team on DIRECTV in their local market, said David Proper, NHL Chief Media Officer and Senior Executive Vice President. "Making it easy for fans to follow their teams is at the heart of what we do. This agreement puts our clubs in four passionate hockey markets in front of more of their fans, and that's a win for everyone who loves the game."

  • Carolina Hurricanes local games are available on channel 650 (streaming, satellite) and 1726/726 (U-verse).
